summary: OpenManus builds exactly one LLM client, the AsyncOpenAI in LLM.__init__, and every one of the five chat.completions calls in app/llm.py (ask, ask_with_images, ask_tool; buffered and streaming) goes through it. That client now passes through the vendored runtime's wrap_openai(), so all five reach Router's /v1/responses when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set and behave exactly as before when it is not. One extra decision was needed: OpenManus ships pointed at Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint rather than OpenAI's (config/config.example.toml), so api.anthropic.com is unlocked as well - a request there goes to Router only when its model is a Router catalog id, and everything else (Azure, Bedrock, local Ollama, the Jiekou/PPIO/Google reseller endpoints, any model Router does not list) still goes to the configured endpoint untouched. All five sites were verified against the real Router: ask buffered and streamed, a two-turn ask_tool loop, and image input, on gpt-4o-mini over api.openai.com and on claude-sonnet-4-5 over api.anthropic.com. The repo's four tests pass with Router on. Two Bedrock calls in app/bedrock.py stay on boto3. Nothing was removed and no behaviour changes until the key is set.
reviewed: The review read every LLM path in the app - the agent loop (BaseAgent.run -> ToolCallAgent.think -> LLM.ask_tool), the vision path, the planning flow, the Bedrock shim and the tenacity retry wrapper - against what Router measurably offers, and checked each candidate change on the live Router where a measurement would settle it. Three were built and tested (a prompt_cache_key for the agent loop's repeated prefix, catalog-driven image support, per-agent spend labels); six more are proposed without branches because each needs a human judgement an apply session should make after approval: which model to run on, which fallback candidates are acceptable mid-run, and how much of the app's own error handling to change.

items.title: Route the shared OpenAI client through Router
items.summary: LLM.__init__'s AsyncOpenAI client passes through wrap_openai(), putting all five app/llm.py chat.completions calls on Router when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set.
items.gains: Every LLM call the app makes through the OpenAI SDK reaches Router: one key instead of a key per vendor, per-request spend and provider reporting, and the Router levers (prompt caching, fallbacks, Flex, spend labels) become available to the policy file. Chat Completions is translated to /v1/responses by the runtime, which Router serves; Router has no Chat Completions endpoint of its own.
items.price: no change by itself: the same model is requested and Router charges catalog list price, which matched the provider's price exactly for gpt-4o-mini and Claude in the fact sheet's measurements.
items.why: This is the whole surface. OpenManus funnels every model call through one LLM class and one client, so a single wrap moves ask, ask_with_images and ask_tool at once - the agent loop included - with no change to how any of them build a request. The runtime is inert until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again, so the switch is an environment variable rather than a deploy. When Router refuses a request before generating, the runtime sends the original request to the provider once, so the provider keys in config.toml stay meaningful.

evidence.detail: A script exercising all five sites (ask buffered, ask streamed, ask_tool, a second ask_tool turn replaying the assistant tool_call and tool result, ask_with_images buffered and streamed) ran against the real Router on gpt-4o-mini: 6 requests, 6 x 200 on /v1/responses, provider=openai, correct answers including the tool round-trip and the image.
The same script against router-sim: 6 requests, 6 valid, 0 invalid, each labelled feature=app/llm.py:<method> client=app/llm.py:__init__.
The repo's test command (compileall + pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/sandbox): 4 passed, the same as the baseline. No test file was changed.
router-migrate check --all: 5 of 7 scanner-visible calls route; the two that do not are the boto3 Bedrock calls (item s1).

items.title: Route Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint too
items.summary: api.anthropic.com is unlocked for the wrapped client, so a request there goes to Router when its model is a Router catalog id.
items.gains: The deployment OpenManus actually ships - the OpenAI SDK pointed at https://api.anthropic.com/v1 - reaches Router. Without this, m1 moves nothing for it: the runtime only routes api.openai.com, and traffic to any other host stays on the provider.
items.loses: For this one host, a request that would have gone to Anthropic on the Anthropic key now goes to Router on the Router key, and Router picks the upstream. The request also stops being Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions call and becomes a Responses call translated by the runtime, so anything that endpoint accepts but Responses does not is no longer available on that path - the runtime keeps such requests on the provider rather than failing, but they then get none of Router's reporting. The commercial relationship for that traffic moves from the Anthropic account to the Router account.
items.price: The catalog price of the resolved model instead of the Anthropic list price. For the dated ids Router maps, these are the same vendor and the same model family; claude-sonnet-4-5 is $3/$15 per 1M on Router, matching Anthropic's list price.
items.why: A Router migration that leaves the shipped configuration entirely on the provider is not a migration. Unlocking is narrow on purpose: it names one host, and the runtime still routes only models that are Router catalog ids, so an unknown or dated id, a local Ollama, or a reseller endpoint is untouched. The failure mode is safe in both directions - if Router refuses, the original request goes to Anthropic once. The hosts deliberately left out are Ollama on localhost (free, local, and its models are not in the catalog) and the Jiekou, PPIO and Google OpenAI-compatible endpoints (operators choose those for their own pricing, and their model ids do not resolve to catalog ids anyway).

evidence.detail: With base_url=https://api.anthropic.com/v1 and model claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929: 4 requests, 4 x 200 on /v1/responses as model=claude-sonnet-4-5, provider=anthropic, covering ask buffered, ask streamed and a two-turn ask_tool loop.

Same host with the shipped example model claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219: ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE recorded every request as to=provider, reason "model 'claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219' is not in the Router catalog". The unlock does not route a model Router cannot serve.
4 passed, same as baseline.

items.title: Operator documentation for the Router switch
items.summary: README gains a short section on turning routing on and off, what routes and what does not, and the trace and model-map variables.
items.gains: Whoever runs this app can see from the README that RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY turns routing on, ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off, the provider keys must stay in config.toml for the fallback path, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE shows where each request went and why.
items.why: The switch is an environment variable with no visible trace in config.toml, which is where an OpenManus operator looks. Undoing this commit removes the documentation and nothing else.

evidence.detail: README.md only; no code touched.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock calls stay on boto3
items.summary: app/bedrock.py talks to bedrock-runtime through boto3, which the runtime does not intercept; those two calls keep going to AWS.
items.why: BedrockClient is a hand-written shim that converts the OpenAI chat shape to Bedrock's converse / converse_stream and signs requests with AWS credentials through boto3. The runtime hooks the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs' HTTP clients, not boto3, and Router does not serve bedrock-runtime with the shared key. Item i7 proposes replacing the shim; it is a rework, not a wrap.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all reports both sites as kept: other SDK / endpoint.

items.title: Azure OpenAI deployments stay on Azure
items.summary: When api_type = "azure", LLM.__init__ builds an AsyncAzureOpenAI client against the customer's Azure endpoint, which the runtime leaves alone.
items.why: The runtime routes requests to api.openai.com and to hosts explicitly unlocked; an Azure resource host is neither, and Azure deployments carry a deployment id rather than a catalog model id. Those installations keep their Azure contract and quota untouched. They could move by pointing config.toml at an OpenAI-shaped base_url with a catalog model, which is a configuration decision for whoever owns the Azure commitment, not a code change.

evidence.detail: The scanner sees no call bound to this client; the runtime's plan_request only matches api.openai.com, unlocked hosts, and api.anthropic.com for Messages.

items.title: Give every routed request a prompt_cache_key
items.summary: router.policy.json sets prompt_cache_key to the request's label, so the agent loop's repeated prefix is cached reliably instead of occasionally.
items.gains: 47% off the input cost of every agent step, measured. An OpenManus step re-sends the Manus system prompt, the whole tool schema set and the entire conversation so far; on a 4,278-token step on gpt-4o-mini the cost went from $0.00068 to $0.00036. Runs get longer as they go, so the saving grows with the run. It also makes caching deterministic rather than luck: without the key, cache hits were 1 of 3 on identical prefixes.
items.loses: The key is the call-site (or, with i3, the agent) label, so it is shared by every concurrent run of that feature. That is what provider affinity wants - it steers same-prefix requests to the same upstream - but it is a routing hint, not isolation, and it does not segregate one user's traffic from another's. Nothing about the request's content or the answer changes. On Claude the runtime already sets this key, so the policy is a no-op there.
items.why: This is the single highest-value lever for an agent: the whole point of the loop is that it re-sends a growing, mostly identical prompt dozens of times. Router charges cache reads at the catalog's cache_read_input rate - $0.075 against $0.15 per 1M on gpt-4o-mini, $0.20 against $2 on claude-sonnet-5 - and the fact sheet records the same effect at -90% for Claude over Responses. It costs one committed JSON file, changes no code, and cannot change an answer.

evidence.detail: Live, gpt-4o-mini, a 4,278-token agent step built from the repo's own Manus system prompt and tool schemas, 3 calls per arm. Without the key: cached 0 / 4,224 / 0 tokens, $0.0006801, $0.0006798, $0.00067995. With the key: cached 4,224 on all three, $0.0003633, $0.000363, $0.00036315.
4 passed on the branch, same as baseline.
router-migrate policy compiled router.policy.json into app/router_policy.py; the compiled copy is committed alongside the JSON so the outside check does not see a stale policy.

items.title: Let the Router catalog decide which models accept images
items.summary: supports_images_for() reads image support from the Router catalog while routing, and base64 images are labelled with their real media type instead of always image/jpeg.
items.gains: Unblocks every modern model for the agent's eyes. MULTIMODAL_MODELS is a hand-kept list that stops at 2024 ids, and a model outside it loses its images silently - format_messages deletes base64_image, so a browser screenshot simply never reaches the model and the agent reasons about a page it cannot see. It also fixes a hard failure the migration would otherwise have introduced: every base64 image is labelled image/jpeg, which OpenAI tolerates and Anthropic rejects outright, so the first Claude model handed a screenshot 400s.
items.loses: Images now reach models that previously had them stripped, which costs input tokens that were not being spent before - on the order of 85 to 1,105 tokens per image by the app's own counter - and changes what those models answer, because they can now see. ask_with_images stops raising for catalog models that take images, so a path that used to fail fast now makes a paid call. The widening applies only while the runtime is active; off Router the original list still decides, so the two paths can disagree about the same model.
items.why: Model choice is the lever Router exists for, and this hardcoded list is what stops the app using it: claude-sonnet-5, gpt-5.4-mini and every other current model would be text-only to OpenManus no matter what the catalog says. The catalog records input modalities per model, so the authority already exists and is current by construction. The media-type fix is not optional alongside it - without it, widening the list just converts silent image loss into a 400.

evidence.detail: claude-sonnet-5, which MULTIMODAL_MODELS does not list, read a 64x64 red/blue PNG correctly through both LLM.ask (base64_image on a message, the shape a tool result uses) and LLM.ask_with_images: 2 requests, 2 x 200, provider=anthropic.

The same test before the media-type fix: 6 x 400 from Anthropic, "The image was specified using the image/jpeg media type, but the image appears to be a image/png image". This is the behaviour the fix removes.

supports_images_for: with the key unset, claude-sonnet-5 False and gpt-4o-mini True (unchanged); with it set, claude-sonnet-5 True, and still False for llama3.2 (not in the catalog) and gpt-oss-120b (text-only in the catalog). Media type detection: PNG, JPEG, GIF, WEBP recognised, anything else keeps the old image/jpeg default.
4 passed on the branch, same as baseline.

items.title: Label Router spend by agent, not by call site
items.summary: BaseAgent.run() scopes its LLM calls to the agent's name and the planning flow to flow.planning; the label travels as x-router-migrate-feature.
items.gains: Spend becomes attributable. Today Manus, the SWE agent, the data-analysis agent, the browser agent and the planning flow all arrive at Router as app/llm.py:ask_tool, so no Router spend view can tell which agent is burning the budget. With per-agent labels you can see it, and because router.policy.json matches on the same label you can then tune per agent - a cheaper model for planning, fallbacks only for the long-running agents, a different cache key per agent - without touching code. It also sharpens i1: a per-agent cache key groups requests that actually share a prefix.
items.loses: The label is a header on every request, including ones that end up at the provider, where it is an unrecognised header the vendor ignores. Agent names become part of the spend record, so renaming an agent splits its history. Anything that calls LLM directly outside an agent run is unlabelled and falls back to the runtime's call-site label, so the two naming schemes coexist in the spend view.
items.why: A gateway's main product is the bill, and an undifferentiated bill is not much of one. OpenManus already has the right boundary - every agent run goes through BaseAgent.run and knows its own name - so the label costs one context manager. The fact sheet notes that whether Router's spend views read this header on Messages traffic is unmeasured; on the Responses path this app uses, the runtime turns the header into metadata.feature, which Router does record.

evidence.detail: A two-step ToolCallAgent run named data_analysis produced 2 requests labelled feature=data_analysis:ask_tool; a call scoped to flow.planning arrived as flow.planning:ask; an unscoped call kept app/llm.py:ask.
4 passed on the branch, same as baseline.

Whether Router's spend dashboard groups by metadata.feature was not checked against the account; the runtime's translation of the header into metadata.feature on /v1/responses is what the simulator confirms.

items.title: Choose the model deliberately instead of inheriting 2025's
items.summary: Map the configured model to a current catalog id via router.policy.json model_map, so the shipped default actually routes and costs less.
items.gains: The shipped default, claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, is not a Router catalog id, so after m1 and m2 an unmodified deployment still sends nothing to Router - the runtime correctly keeps it on Anthropic. A model_map entry is what closes that gap. It is also a straight price cut: claude-sonnet-5 is $2/$10 per 1M against claude-3-7-sonnet's $3/$15, on a newer model; for the cheap paths claude-haiku-5-5 is $0.10/$0.50, a 30x cut on input. The vision config can be mapped separately from the main one.
items.loses: A different model gives different answers, and nothing offline measures whether they are better for this agent. An agent loop is unusually sensitive to this: tool-calling discipline, when to stop, and how it recovers from a failed tool all shift with the model, and a change that reads as neutral on single prompts can change how often a run finishes. It also overrides a model the operator chose explicitly, which is surprising unless it is documented where they configured it.
items.why: This is the decision a human should make, not an agent: it depends on the deployment's actual config.toml (unknown from the repo - config.toml is not committed) and on how much answer drift the owner will accept. What can be said is that the shipped default is on neither Router nor the current Anthropic line-up, and that the three obvious targets are claude-sonnet-5 (same class, cheaper), claude-haiku-5-5 (far cheaper, lighter) and gpt-5.4-mini (cheaper, and the only one of the three with a Flex tier, where the fact sheet measures exactly -50%). An apply session should write the map for the model the deployment actually runs, after someone picks a target.

items.title: Fall over to a second model instead of ending the run
items.summary: A fallbacks list in router.policy.json lets Router retry an agent step on another model in-request, rather than the app burning six backoff retries and giving up.
items.gains: An OpenManus run is ten to thirty sequential model calls, and any one failing ends it. Today the only recovery is tenacity: six attempts with exponential backoff up to 60s each, all to the same model, so a provider outage costs minutes and then loses the run and everything it had done. A Router fallbacks list moves recovery inside the request - Router falls through a model that is down, refused, or rejecting a parameter, silently and immediately.
items.loses: The reply can come from a different model mid-run, and the response does not say which candidate served, so an agent run can silently change its reasoning style halfway through; for a loop that depends on consistent tool discipline that can be worse than a clean failure. Fallbacks also disable Flex (Router ignores allow_flex_tier when a models list is present), so a Flex-eligible model loses its discount on these requests, and the least capable candidate caps the tools, structured output and modalities the whole request may use. Truncated attempts are still billed.
items.why: Reliability is the lever this app needs most after cost, because the unit of work is a whole run rather than one answer. The reason it is proposed rather than built is that the candidate list cannot be written without knowing the configured model, and the right list is a same-class model that supports tools and images (claude-sonnet-5 next to claude-sonnet-4-6, or gpt-5.4-mini next to gpt-5-mini) - not a cheap one, which would turn an outage into a quietly worse run. The fact sheet records fallback behaviour on real provider outages as documented but not measured, so this should go out behind a dashboard approval with the first week watched.

items.title: Stop retrying errors that cannot succeed
items.summary: The tenacity wrapper retries every exception six times, including request errors and the token-limit guard; narrow it to the errors a retry can actually fix.
items.gains: Cuts wasted calls and the worst-case wait. retry_if_exception_type((OpenAIError, Exception, ValueError)) matches everything, so a malformed request is sent six times with up to 60s of backoff between attempts - about five minutes before the agent gives up on an error that was never going to change. On Router each of those attempts can also trigger the runtime's one provider retry, doubling the upstream traffic. Narrowing it to rate limits, timeouts and 5xx keeps the retries that help and drops the ones that only cost money and time.
items.loses: Errors that currently succeed on a later attempt by luck would start surfacing immediately, so some runs that limp through today would fail faster and more visibly. TokenLimitExceeded would arrive as itself rather than wrapped in a RetryError, which means the unwrapping in ToolCallAgent.think (it checks e.__cause__) has to be updated in the same change or it stops recognising the case.
items.why: It is the app's own error handling, but Router is what makes the waste visible and chargeable: during this migration a single ask() call with a bad image produced six identical 400s at Router in a row, which is exactly the pattern. It is proposed rather than built because changing retry semantics changes which runs survive, and the comment in the code ("Don't retry TokenLimitExceeded") shows the current behaviour was not intended - which means someone should decide what was, rather than an agent guessing.

items.title: Derive the reasoning-model list from the catalog
items.summary: REASONING_MODELS is ["o1", "o3-mini"]; read the catalog's reasoning flag instead, and send reasoning_effort where the model supports it.
items.gains: Every current reasoning model - gpt-5.x, o3, o4-mini, the Claude Opus and Sonnet line - is missing from that list, so the app sends them max_tokens and temperature instead of max_completion_tokens. On Router the runtime rescues both (it maps either cap to max_output_tokens and drops temperature on the 36 catalog ids whose catalog says temperature: false), but the provider-fallback path has no such rescue and gets a 400 from the vendor. Reading the catalog fixes the fallback path and, more usefully, makes reasoning_effort available: today it is never sent, so reasoning models always run at their default effort, with no way to buy accuracy on a hard step or save tokens on an easy one.
items.loses: Sending reasoning_effort changes output length, latency and cost on every reasoning model, and on Claude it needs at least about 1,100 output tokens or the request 400s on thinking.enabled.budget_tokens - so it cannot simply be switched on for the app's smaller max_tokens settings without a guard.
items.why: Same shape as i2: a hand-kept list that the catalog already knows better, and the thing standing between this app and the models Router sells. Smaller than i2 because the runtime is already covering for it on the routed path - which is also why it is a quick-win rather than urgent.

items.title: Take token counts from Router instead of estimating them
items.summary: Use the usage Router returns (and usage.cost on Responses) rather than tiktoken estimates for streaming completions and the input budget.
items.gains: Makes the app's own accounting true. ask() estimates streamed completion tokens by re-encoding the text with tiktoken, and the max_input_tokens budget is built on tiktoken's cl100k_base encoding for every model - which is simply the wrong tokenizer for Claude, Gemini and the open-weight models, so the budget that stops a runaway agent is enforced against a number that does not match the bill. Router returns exact usage on every response and a usage.cost in dollars on Responses, which the runtime already passes back through the chat-shaped reply.
items.loses: Streaming usage only arrives if the app asks for it (stream_options.include_usage), and it arrives at the end of the stream, so a budget check that must happen before the request still needs an estimate. The fact sheet also records Messages token counts as wrong for Fireworks-served models and different per surface on grok, so exact-from-Router is exact for the path this app uses, not universally.
items.why: An agent that cannot measure its own spend cannot be governed, and this app ships a budget feature built on a guess. Low risk, no answer changes, and it turns usage.cost into something the logs can report per run - which is what makes i1's and i4's savings visible to whoever approved them.

items.title: Retire the Bedrock shim in favour of Router's Bedrock ids
items.summary: Replace app/bedrock.py's 334-line boto3 OpenAI-shape emulator with a plain client on Router, which lists the same Bedrock models.
items.gains: Deletes a hand-written translation layer that reimplements OpenAI's chat and tool-call shapes over bedrock-runtime converse / converse_stream, including a module-level global for the current tool-use id with a "Tmp solution" comment - a real correctness hazard under concurrency. Router's catalog carries the same models (us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5, global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, us.openai.gpt-6-luna and more), so api_type = "aws" could become an ordinary client on Router and inherit everything the other paths get: caching, fallbacks, spend labels, usage.cost.
items.loses: Bedrock ids on Router are BYOK - they need the caller's AWS credentials registered on the Router account, so this does not remove the AWS relationship, it moves where the credential lives, and a deployment whose whole reason for Bedrock is that traffic must stay inside its own AWS account may not accept that. Bedrock-specific behaviour the shim exposes (guardrails, inference profiles, region pinning) is not reachable through Router. It is also the only item here that deletes a file, so it needs real testing on an AWS deployment, which this repo's tests do not cover.
items.why: It is the last LLM path not on Router, and the one carrying the most incidental code. The reason it is a rework and not a change is that the trade is not purely technical: it asks a Bedrock customer to put their AWS credential on the Router account. Worth doing if the answer is yes, and worth leaving alone if it is no.

items.title: Flex stays at the account default
items.summary: No service tier is forced on any request, so Flex-eligible OpenAI models keep the account's cost-efficient routing.
items.price: The fact sheet measures Flex at exactly -50% on gpt-5.4-mini, with latency indistinguishable from standard over five calls - but also records one gpt-5-nano Flex call that took 61 seconds.
items.why: Nothing in this migration sets service_tier or allow_flex_tier, so Router's account default applies, which is cost-efficient routing. That is the right default for this app: no OpenManus path has a hard latency budget, and the user is already waiting on a multi-step agent run. It is written down because it is a decision by omission - if a latency outlier on an interactive step becomes a complaint, the fix is service_tier: "default" on that feature in router.policy.json, and if it does not, the discount is already being taken. Claude has no tiers on Router, so this only applies to deployments configured for OpenAI models.

evidence.detail: Not measured on this account: the live checks used gpt-4o-mini, which has no Flex tier, and claude-sonnet-4-5, which has none either. The -50% figure is the fact sheet's measurement on gpt-5.4-mini.
